blocks.text: Paul Dirac predicted in 1928 that the fundamental particles have their antiparticles. The rest masses of the antiparticles are the same as those of their corresponding particles, but their charges are opposite. For example, the positron is the antiparticle of the electron, represented by e+; its rest mass is the same as that of an electron, but it carries a positive charge of the same magnitude. The positron was the first antiparticle discovered, by Anderson in 1932 in a cloud chamber experiment; this was the first experimental discovery of an antiparticle, and many antiparticles were discovered after that. An antiparticle is usually represented by a letter with a bar over it, for example the antiproton p-bar and the antineutrino nu-bar.

Quarks and leptons have been recognized as the fundamental particles, also known as elementary particles, among the very many particles discovered, and these elementary particles also have antiparticles. For their work on this discovery, Dirac and Anderson received the Nobel Prize in Physics, Dirac in 1933 and Anderson in 1936; in 1955 Segre and Chamberlain discovered the antiproton using a particle accelerator and were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1959 (Interesting Information). A particle accelerator is a huge machine that accelerates charged particles such as electrons, protons or ions to extremely high energies and speeds approaching the speed of light; linear accelerators, cyclotrons and betatrons are important particle accelerators (For Your Information).

items: Cosmic rays are high-energy particles coming from outer space with unknown sources, perhaps the Sun or other stars. They consist mostly of protons, neutrons and heavier nuclei, which continually bombard the Earth; when they interact with the atoms of the gases of the atmosphere they produce showers of secondary particles that rain down on us all the time.

When nuclei of an unstable radioactive element such as uranium-235 undergo fission in nuclear reactors, they emit a variety of particles, such as neutrons, neutrinos, alpha particles, photons, electrons and positrons.

When charged particles such as electrons and protons are accelerated and made to bombard a target material such as hydrogen, they may also collide head-on with each other; the debris from these reactions contains particles like pions, kaons, muons and even antiprotons.

blocks.text: Pair production occurs when a gamma-ray photon (a high-energy photon) passes near an atomic nucleus: an electron-positron pair is emitted (Fig. 12.1). The presence of a third particle, such as a nucleus, is necessary to conserve linear momentum, so pair production cannot take place in empty space (Do You Know). According to mass-energy equivalence, the minimum energy of the photon must equal the sum of the rest mass energies of the created particles: 2 m0 c^2 = 1.02 MeV for the electron-positron pair, which has been verified experimentally. A gamma-ray photon with energy less than 1.02 MeV cannot produce an electron-positron pair, whereas a photon with more than 1.02 MeV creates a pair and the excess energy goes into the kinetic energies of the particles. Pair production satisfies the laws of conservation of charge, momentum and energy.

Annihilation is the opposite process to pair production. When an electron and a positron interact, they annihilate into two gamma-ray photons (Fig. 12.2, cited as Fig. 12.4 in print): e- + e+ -> gamma + gamma. The energy of each gamma-ray photon is 0.51 MeV, equal to the rest mass energy of an electron or a positron, E = m0 c^2. In an annihilation reaction energy and momentum are conserved. Besides electron-positron annihilation, the annihilation of other particles and their antiparticles can also occur, such as proton and antiproton, lepton and antilepton, quark and antiquark. High-energy collisions between particles at CERN have revealed that some of the mass of colliding particles is changed into electromagnetic radiation according to Einstein's equation, and the leftover mass appears as new subatomic particles (Fig. 12.3, a high-energy proton-proton collision producing 18 new particles).

blocks.prompt: Can there be pair production for photons of energy 20 keV (short question 12.8)? Why can an electron-positron pair not decay into a single photon (short question 12.13)?
blocks.explanation: No. Producing an electron and a positron needs at least 2 m0 c^2 = 1.02 MeV, and 20 keV is far less. A single photon cannot carry away the momentum: in the frame where the pair is at rest its total momentum is zero, but a single photon always has momentum E/c, so momentum and energy could not both be conserved; two photons moving in opposite directions can share the energy with zero total momentum.

blocks.prompt: What is the difference between matter and antimatter (comprehensive question 12.3)? Explain pair annihilation with an example and its use in medicine (comprehensive question 12.4).
blocks.explanation: An antiparticle has the same mass as its particle but opposite charge (and opposite magnetic properties): the positron is the electron's antiparticle, the antiproton the proton's; antimatter is made of antiparticles. When a particle meets its antiparticle they annihilate, their mass turning into energy; an electron and a positron give two 0.51 MeV gamma photons travelling in opposite directions. In positron emission tomography (PET) a patient receives a tracer that emits positrons; each positron annihilates with an electron in the body, and detectors around the patient pick up the pairs of opposite gamma photons to map where the tracer has collected.

items: Dirac (1928): each particle has an antiparticle, same rest mass, opposite charge; positron e+ found by Anderson (1932); antiproton by Segre and Chamberlain (1955). Accelerators, cosmic rays and fission produce many particles.

Pair production: a gamma photon of at least 1.02 MeV near a nucleus gives e- and e+. Annihilation: e- + e+ -> 2 gamma, each 0.51 MeV; charge, momentum and energy conserved; at CERN some mass becomes radiation and the rest new particles.
